frameworks.name: MAYA (Maximally Advanced Yet Acceptable)
frameworks.definition: A product or design should be as novel as possible while remaining within the threshold of consumer acceptance; evolution is preferred over revolution because consumers migrate behavior rather than reinvent it.

frameworks.name: Consistent-Distinctive-Famous Brand Framework
frameworks.definition: Three-part brand-building framework: (1) be consistent across all touchpoints over time, (2) be distinctive in visual and experiential identity, and (3) pursue fame as a non-linear multiplier that changes the rules of every interaction.

frameworks.name: Psychological-Technological-Economic Parallel Design
frameworks.definition: Great products satisfy all three criteria simultaneously in parallel, not in series: works psychologically (people want it), works technologically (can be made), and works economically (can generate profit). Most companies run these in series, losing integration benefits.

frameworks.name: Persian Dual-State Deliberation
frameworks.definition: According to Herodotus, ancient Persians debated major decisions twice: once sober and once drunk. A decision was adopted only if it passed both states, ensuring it survived both rational scrutiny and emotional/intuitive review.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that when successful products are evaluated in hindsight, observers systematically forget the role marketing played in their adoption and attribute success solely to product quality. This creates a survivorship bias that leads future product designers to underinvest in marketing and positioning.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Hindsight causes post-rationalization: people say they bought a product because it was great, when actually they believed it was great because of the marketing. The marketing becomes invisible in memory, leaving only the product.
bounded_by: Mobile phone adoption was partly driven by social pressure, not purely marketing — a partial exception where network effects overcame normal adoption resistance

claims.text: Rory Sutherland asserts that brand fame operates non-linearly and reaches escape velocity thresholds where the rules of business change qualitatively: famous companies receive unsolicited inbound applications from customers and employees, get the benefit of the doubt when mistakes occur, and face lower due-diligence barriers in B2B sales — advantages that cannot be quantified because the counterfactual (operating unfamous) is unobservable.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Fame functions like a trust proxy — when a brand is recognized, counterparties (buyers, employees, partners) skip verification steps they would otherwise perform, reducing friction across every business interaction simultaneously.
bounded_by: Fame must be matched to the relevant audience — luxury car prestige requires the prestige signal to be recognized by the people who observe your purchase, not just by you

claims.text: Rory Sutherland claims that brand-building marketing activity is systematically undervalued by approximately 4x when measured on short-term transactional metrics, because brand value compounds via power laws and non-linearities rather than linear addition — the mathematics used to evaluate it (ROI, quarter-by-quarter revenue contribution) is structurally incapable of capturing its actual contribution.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Applies to brand-building activities vs. direct-response advertising measured over short time frames
claims.mechanism: Brand value accumulates compoundingly like a pension: early contributions appear small or negative, but compound into disproportionate value over years. Linear ROI math cannot capture power-law accumulation.

numbers.axis: Estimated true value of brand-building marketing relative to short-term measured contribution

anchors.region: Rory Sutherland estimate of actual contribution

bounded_by: This is Rory Sutherland's rough estimate, explicitly acknowledged as plucked from the air; the actual multiplier could be higher

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that idiosyncratic product features and slight frictions — things a standup comedian might mock — are disproportionately valuable for brand distinctiveness. These small oddities create disproportionate attention and memorability precisely because they deviate from consumer expectation.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Idiosyncrasies must remain within the MAYA (maximally advanced yet acceptable) threshold — too weird causes rejection
claims.mechanism: Slight deviations from expected patterns attract disproportionate attention because human perception is tuned to notice pattern breaks, not patterns. A step that is slightly off-height on a staircase gets noticed; uniform steps do not.
bounded_by: Features that are too strange or require behavior reinvention (not evolution) can create rejection rather than memorability

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the MAYA (maximally advanced yet acceptable) principle governs successful product innovation: consumers accept evolution of behavior but resist complete reinvention. Products that are the right amount of unfamiliar — enough to generate interest but not so foreign as to require wholesale behavioral change — succeed over those that are either too conventional or too radical.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Applies to consumer-facing product innovation; does not necessarily apply to B2B infrastructure where switching costs dominate adoption decisions
claims.mechanism: Consumers prefer to migrate existing behaviors into new formats rather than abandoning prior behaviors entirely. Products that allow behavioral migration have lower psychological adoption barriers than those requiring behavioral reinvention.
bounded_by: The iPhone was partially a freak exception — however, it was preceded by iPod adoption, which provided a behavioral stepping stone

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that social copying (doing what others do) and habit (doing what one has done before) are the two dominant default behavioral modes in humans, and both are evolutionarily rational as low-variance, low-downside heuristics. Attempts to persuade consumers via rational economic argument frequently fail because they address neither mode.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: do what everybody else seems to be doing
claims.mechanism: An organism that learns everything from first principles would make fatal errors in novel environments. Social copying and habit provide low-cost access to accumulated group knowledge about safe behaviors, making them preferable to individual calculation under uncertainty.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that real-world business decisions — especially those involving human behavior — violate every condition required for scientific decision-making: they have multiple right answers (not single), the information available is incomplete and some is irrelevant, outcomes are non-proportionate to inputs, and the past is an unreliable guide. Selecting and promoting managers on their ability to perform logical linear reasoning therefore systematically selects for a skill that is largely inapplicable to actual business problems.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Applies to decisions involving human behavior; does not apply to engineering, manufacturing, or other deterministic domains where linear proportionality holds
bounded_by: Engineering and manufacturing contexts where linear proportionality does hold are explicitly excluded

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the ability to behave unpredictably is meta-rationally advantageous in adversarial negotiation contexts (such as New York real estate), because a fully predictable, consistently logical counterparty can be modeled and exploited by opponents who learn to anticipate their moves.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Contexts where opponents can model and exploit predictable behavior (real estate, game-theoretic negotiations)
claims.mechanism: A party that is fully predictable can be gamed: opponents learn to anticipate responses and structure their offers accordingly. Introducing unpredictability raises opponent uncertainty, improving negotiating position.
bounded_by: Does not apply to contexts requiring trust and reliability (supplier relationships, employment, partnerships) where consistent behavior builds valuable reputation

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the primary barrier to adoption of genuinely superior products is psychological and social rather than functional, and that otherwise excellent products can permanently fail to cross the adoption threshold if the user imagery associated with early adopters is unappealing to mainstream buyers.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Consumer-facing products where purchases signal identity or group membership
claims.mechanism: Consumers evaluate products partly through social proof (what kind of person uses this?) and those who do not want to affiliate with the early-adopter profile will resist adoption even when the product is functionally superior.
bounded_by: Does not apply to B2B products where purchase decisions are less tied to user identity signaling

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that electric vehicles in the UK and similar markets have been systematically slowed in mainstream adoption because environmental messaging has stigmatized EV owners as smug and condescending, causing non-EV owners to avoid purchase to avoid being associated with that identity — despite the fact that most actual EV buyers are motivated by technology enthusiasm and novelty rather than environmental conviction.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Consumer adoption of technology products in markets where environmental positioning is politically polarizing
claims.mechanism: Brand association creates identity signals. When a product becomes associated with a disliked reference group (smug environmentalists), members of groups who do not want that identity actively avoid the product, even when they would otherwise find it appealing on functional grounds.
bounded_by: In areas without political polarization around environmentalism the same dynamic may not apply

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the first adopters of any innovative technology tend to be slightly unusual people, and that unusual people do not confer mainstream social reassurance to subsequent potential buyers — creating a paradox where the people most likely to adopt early are precisely the people whose adoption retards mainstream uptake.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: weird people do not confer the reassurance of social norms
conditions: Consumer technology products where social norms and risk-reduction through peer adoption are key purchase drivers
claims.mechanism: Social proof works via similarity: mainstream consumers take cues from people like themselves. Early adopters (who are by definition outliers) signal that the product is for unusual people, which repels rather than attracts mainstream adoption.
bounded_by: Mobile phone adoption was unusual in that social pressure (network effects from friends having phones) overcame this barrier; mobile phones became a requirement rather than a lifestyle choice

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that restricting a product to a single clearly defined function — rather than adding low-cost features that expand functionality — can increase rather than decrease consumer value, because multi-function products create ambiguity about what the product is for, which raises the cognitive cost of decision and reduces willingness to purchase.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: one function which it performs very well
conditions: Consumer products where the core use case is clear and a single compelling function is the purchase driver
claims.mechanism: Functional ambiguity raises decision cost: a buyer who must decide how they will use a device across multiple possible use cases has a harder decision than one who simply answers 'do I want to do this one thing?' The simplicity of binary decisions improves conversion.
bounded_by: Does not apply to platform or productivity products where multi-functionality is the core value proposition (e.g. smartphones themselves)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that small, autonomous team structures of approximately 10 people outperform large-unit management structures on both employee motivation and customer experience, because natural human instincts of reciprocity and obligation do not scale effectively beyond the Dunbar number threshold — and critically, they function strongly at the 10-person sports-team scale.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Service businesses with customer-facing teams; not tested for manufacturing or purely transactional contexts
claims.mechanism: Reciprocity and obligation are human instincts that activate strongly in small groups. When a team member is absent from a 10-person team, each remaining member absorbs 10%+ extra load and feels the impact personally. In 100-person units, individual absence is diffuse and invisible, so social pressure for attendance dissolves.

numbers.axis: Team size and activation of reciprocity-based motivation

anchors.value: ~150 people (maximum where social familiarity is maintained)
1 manager : 100 staff (reciprocity obligations diffuse and ineffective)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that quantitative performance metrics in customer-facing roles create two systematic failure modes: (1) employees game the metrics to their own advantage while failing customers, or (2) employees comply with metrics but feel demotivated by the loss of discretionary judgment — and both failure modes are more costly than the variance the metrics were designed to eliminate.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Customer-facing service roles where quality involves human judgment (call centers, customer service, hospitality)
claims.mechanism: Metrics eliminate the discretionary autonomy that gives work human meaning. Workers who exercise no judgment feel fundamentally dehumanized, reducing intrinsic motivation. Simultaneously, when compensation depends on metrics, rational employees optimize the metric rather than the underlying goal the metric was supposed to proxy.
bounded_by: Rory Sutherland does not claim metrics are never useful — they are appropriate in manufacturing or deterministic processes where the output can be fully specified

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that product failures should not be permanently written off after a single failed launch, because timing, user imagery, and marketing execution are often the causal variables rather than the product itself — and these variables can change without the product changing.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: don't think because a product's failed in the past that you shouldn't try again
bounded_by: Retrying with identical marketing and timing is uninformative — the retry must change one of the causal variables (timing, user imagery, marketing channel, positioning)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that marketing professionals are systematically higher in openness to experience than the general population, which creates a dangerous blind spot: marketers who follow their own preferences and instincts will consistently design for a small minority of consumers who share their openness profile, rather than for the majority who are driven primarily by habit, social norms, and the desire to fit in.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: people in marketing are very high in openness

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that in B2B contexts, brand fame creates an asymmetric accountability transfer: when a company is famous (IBM, PricewaterhouseCoopers), any negative outcomes from the decision to hire them are attributed to the vendor; when an unknown company is hired, negative outcomes are attributed to the decision-maker who hired them. This asymmetry makes famous vendors dramatically easier to sell and dramatically harder to displace.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: no one ever got fired for buying IBM
conditions: B2B procurement decisions where the buyer has internal accountability for vendor selection
claims.mechanism: Famous brands absorb blame for failures; unknown brands transfer blame to the buyer. Risk-averse buyers (the majority in large organizations) therefore rationally prefer famous vendors even when unknown vendors offer better terms, because the personal downside of a failed experiment is higher.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that when businesses and governments use AI to understand behavior change, AI-identified drivers of adoption differ systematically from what rational economic models predict. A concrete example: an AI investigating heat pump adoption found that the single most persuasive factor was knowing that three neighbors already had one — not environmental benefits, cost savings calculations, or government incentives.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: three people on their street had a heat pump
conditions: Consumer adoption of home technology products (heat pumps, solar panels) in residential settings
claims.mechanism: Social proof from geographic proximity activates the social copying heuristic: observing that same-street neighbors have adopted safely removes the first-mover downside risk in the observer's mind, lowering adoption barriers more effectively than rational argument.

numbers.axis: Number of same-street neighbors with heat pump required to trigger adoption consideration

anchors.value: Low adoption intent (resisting being first mover)
Single most persuasive adoption trigger identified by AI analysis

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that early technology adopters among the wealthy perform an economically essential function: they provide the early-stage demand and revenue that funds technology maturation, enabling prices to fall and quality to improve for mass-market adoption. This is an argument against the common view of early adopters as foolish status-seekers.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.speaker_term: early stage funding for promising ideas
conditions: Physical consumer technology products (cars, electronics, home appliances) that require capital investment to achieve manufacturing scale
claims.mechanism: Early adopters pay premium prices that fund manufacturing scale-up and product iteration. Without their willingness to pay a premium for an immature product, the product cannot achieve the volume needed to reduce unit costs to mass-market levels.
bounded_by: Does not apply to digital products with near-zero marginal cost, where early-adopter pricing is less critical to scale-up economics

examples.text: Veuve Clicquot's yellow label originated as a printing error. The champagne house initially planned to sell the misprinted bottles in England rather than France, treating the distinctive yellow lame label as a defect. English customers subsequently requested more of the champagne specifically identified as 'the one with the yellow label.' The house then deliberately intensified the yellow, turning an accidental imperfection into the brand's most recognizable identifier. The entire brand identity of Veuve Clicquot — one of the world's best-known champagne houses — is traceable to a printing mistake that was retained rather than corrected.

Jaguar in the 1990s had a reading light activated by a switch on the central console rather than a switch above the light itself — the opposite of every other car. Ogilvy's creative director told Jaguar to preserve this oddity as a mark of distinctiveness. Jaguar was actually planning to eliminate the feature as inconsistent. The example illustrates that brand-building sometimes requires deliberately keeping things that optimization would remove.

Rolls Royce historically used a floor pedal to dip headlamps rather than the stalk used by all other manufacturers. The idiosyncratic control survived across generations of a product known for obsessive attention to refinement, functioning as a signature tactile experience that distinguished the car from competitors at the most intimate interaction level.

MCI's Friends and Family program in US telephony allowed subscribers to nominate a set of frequently-called numbers (initially 10, later expanded to 25) that received a 20% discount. The program required customers to actively specify their own network — adding friction relative to a blanket 15-20% price reduction. It generated disproportionately more consumer interest and comedy-material attention than a flat price cut of equivalent value would have, illustrating that slight friction and personalization can increase engagement beyond what rational price equivalence would predict.

The Danish crime series The Killing was purchased by a BBC4 commissioning editor for £24,000 (approximately $30,000) after airing on Danish state television. The buyer's stated rationale: Scandinavian content is 'just the right amount of weird' for British viewers — similar enough to be comprehensible but different enough to be interesting. The series subsequently migrated to BBC2 and Netflix acquired the rights, generating tens of millions of pounds for the original Danish broadcaster from a £24,000 initial sale. The example illustrates MAYA: the right distance from the familiar generates outsized engagement.

The Meta Portal TV was, by Rory Sutherland's assessment, a £500 piece of technology sold for approximately $120 — roughly exceptional value. Reviews consistently praised the device's functionality. Yet every review opened with seven to nine paragraphs of privacy concern about allowing a Facebook camera in the home, followed by a single paragraph acknowledging the product's quality. The device was discontinued despite its functional superiority. Sutherland uses this as an example of a product that failed due to its association with a brand (Facebook) generating trust concerns — a psychological failure, not a product failure.

Edward Jenner's cowpox-based smallpox vaccination faced opposition comparable in intensity to modern anti-vaccination movements despite smallpox being one of the 17th and 18th centuries' most devastating diseases. Jenner's marketing breakthrough was persuading the British royal family to vaccinate their children — an early use of celebrity social proof to overcome mass resistance to a demonstrably beneficial innovation. Sutherland uses this to illustrate that successful product adoption almost always requires explicit marketing and social-proof intervention, not just product quality.

Akio Morita (Sony) insisted the original Walkman have only one function: listening to high-quality music. Adding a recording microphone (feasible for approximately $0.50 per unit) was rejected despite doubling functional capability. Morita's argument: once the device had more than one function, consumers would be uncertain what it was for, raising decision cost and reducing conversion. The Walkman became a category-defining product precisely because its singular purpose was unambiguous. Sutherland uses this as the canonical example of less-is-more in product design.

Zappos' customer service team refused to implement speed metrics for call center staff. The brief was: calls last as long as needed to solve the customer's problem. One recorded customer service call lasted seven hours. Sutherland uses this as an example of a company that correctly identified that eliminating discretionary judgment destroys intrinsic motivation, and that the resulting dehumanization is more costly than the variance that metrics were designed to reduce.

Shopify's customer service teams were organized into groups of 10, modeled by COO Toby Shannon on sports teams. This required a team leader for every 10 people rather than one manager for 100, making the structure less lean in conventional terms. The result: staff reported extraordinary job satisfaction and motivation, and crucially, kept each other motivated because the team was small enough for each individual's absence to be visibly felt by teammates — activating reciprocity and obligation at the appropriate social scale.

Google Glass was launched first to developers as early adopters. Developers — by Sutherland's characterization not the world's coolest people — were seen wearing the glasses in bars and other social settings. This created unfavorable user imagery for mainstream adoption: the product became associated with a reference group that mainstream consumers did not want to resemble. The product failed despite Sutherland's personal assessment that it was functionally compelling at any price. The example illustrates that user imagery established during early adoption can be permanently disqualifying.

Electric car adoption in parts of England revealed an unexpected geographic pattern: areas stereotyped as environmentally progressive (Cambridge, Brighton) had few charging stations, while areas associated with car culture and status display (Essex, upmarket shopping destinations) had abundant charging infrastructure. Sutherland argues this reflects that actual EV adoption in the UK is driven by technology enthusiasm and status display, not environmental conviction — and that the environmental messaging attached to EVs has created a harmful brand association that repels mainstream buyers who do not want to signal environmental virtue.

Wrigley began as a soap powder company in Chicago. He gave away baking powder free to incentivize soap powder sales. He then pivoted to sell baking powder directly. He then gave away chewing gum as a free gift with baking powder purchases. Customers preferred the chewing gum to the baking powder. Wrigley became a chewing gum company. Sutherland uses this example to illustrate that real innovation processes are non-linear pivots, not the tidy linear stories we tell in hindsight — and that attempts to force business decision processes into linear models creates a mismatch with the actual nature of discovery.

Rory Sutherland signed out a mobile phone from his employer's fleet in 1989 and received abuse shouted from passing cars while using it on Oxford Street. In approximately 1994-1995 he was making an international call on his own mobile phone on the top of a London bus and feared physical attack for the social provocation of an international mobile call in a public setting. He uses these first-person experiences to illustrate that the timeline of behavioral normalization for new technologies is measured in years or decades, not months, and that what feels socially outrageous in one era is unremarkable in the next.

practices.text: When developing a new product or service, run three parallel tests simultaneously rather than in series: (1) does it work psychologically — do people actually want it and does it feel right? (2) does it work technologically — can it be built or delivered? (3) does it work economically — can it generate profit? Treat any failure in one dimension as equally disqualifying as failure in another.

When assessing a failed product concept for revival, identify which causal variable failed (timing, user imagery, marketing channel, positioning, or functionality) and change only that variable in the retry. Do not reuse identical launch strategy and expect different results.

For early-stage brand building, pursue three priorities in parallel: consistency (maintain visual and experiential identity without frequent changes), distinctiveness (preserve or amplify idiosyncratic features rather than normalizing them), and fame (pursue being known in your target market as a primary objective, not a byproduct of other activities).

When structuring product teams or customer service teams, use groups of approximately 10 rather than large units managed by a single supervisor. The smaller team size activates natural human reciprocity and obligation that sustains motivation without requiring metric-based incentive systems.

When designing innovation processes in organizations, create a double-lock deliberation: first allow rational analysis to proceed to its conclusion, then separately create protected time for non-rational, lateral, or 'silly' idea generation. Require both types of review before committing to a course of action.
